title: The History of the Two Worlds: a Kentish physician, the Rose Cross, and the quarrel over how nature is read
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Milgate House, Bearsted: the treasurer's third son
stops.date_confidence: day and month attested in the DNB and Wikipedia; the identification of the birth house as Milgate is genealogical tradition, and the coordinate is the house rather than the village centre at 51.2738, 0.5789
stops.campa: Sir Thomas Fludd, treasurer-at-war to Elizabeth in the Low Countries and afterwards member for Kent, keeps a house at Milgate in the parish of Bearsted, under the downs. He counts army money for a queen who has been paying for a war in the Netherlands for a decade. His third son will spend a life counting a different order of things, the correspondences that tie a man's body to the heavens. That son is born at Milgate on the seventeenth of January, 1574, and christened Robert.
suggested_refs: Milgate House, Bearsted, seat of Sir Thomas Fludd
Holy Cross Church, Bearsted, where the same family is buried

stops.name: St John's College, Oxford: a commoner at seventeen
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He enters St John's as a commoner in 1591 and stays six years over the arts course. The Medical Fellow in residence is Matthew Gwinne, who practises Galenic medicine and has written a tract showing he has read the principal Paracelsian work as well. Two doctrines sit in one college, and in one man's library. Fludd will spend forty years arguing that the second is the deeper of them. Did Gwinne ever put the question to the undergraduate from Kent? The records do not say.
suggested_refs: Matthew Gwinne's tract on Galenic and Paracelsian medicine
The buttery books of St John's College, Oxford, 1591-1598

stops.name: Oxford: the bachelor's degree and a disputed year
stops.date_confidence: contested: Wikipedia gives 1597, the DNB quotes the Oxford register for 3 February 1596. Old-style dating would reconcile the two, but no consulted source performs that reconciliation, so the year is left open
stops.campa: The degree is taken and the year of it is not settled. One account has him bachelor of arts in 1597; the Oxford register the Victorian dictionary quotes puts it at the third of February, 1596. England still turns its year at Lady Day in March, which would make both entries the same winter under two names. No source consulted performs that reconciliation, so the two dates stand side by side, unreconciled. He proceeds master of arts the following year.
stops.quote_source: Oxford University records, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), 'Fludd, Robert'
suggested_refs: The Oxford University register of degrees, 1596-1598

stops.name: Oxford: master of arts, and out of England
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the departure for the Continent follows shortly after, undated
stops.campa: He proceeds master of arts in 1598 and goes abroad for roughly six years. The whole documentary record of those years is one clause in a Victorian dictionary entry: France, Spain, Italy and Germany, and teaching in noble families. Everything else said about the journey, the Jesuits in the mountains, the Guise boys and their mathematics, is his own later recollection or somebody's reasonable guess laid over a blank. He leaves an English graduate in arts and comes back a physician of another school.
stops.quote: visiting France, Spain, Italy, and Germany, and teaching in noble families
suggested_refs: The DNB's single-clause summary of the continental years, the whole documentary basis for six years of travel

stops.name: The Pyrenees: a winter of theurgy
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Fludd's own later recollection as relayed by Wikipedia. No town is named and no year is fixed, so the coordinate marks the range and the date marks a winter within 1598-1600
stops.campa: By his own account, told long afterward, he spends a winter in the mountains between France and Spain with Jesuit teachers, studying theurgy: the working of ritual upon the orders of angels. What he brings down out of the passes is a conviction he never afterwards puts down, that the invisible orders can be addressed and will answer. He is twenty-four. No town is named. No month is given. The record is one man remembering, decades later, a season spent learning from priests of a church his own country had outlawed.
suggested_refs: Fludd's autobiographical remarks on the Pyrenean winter, surviving only in summary

stops.name: Avignon: tutor to the house of Guise
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the DNB alone, uncorroborated, and undated within roughly 1600-1601
stops.campa: Tradition puts him at Avignon in the papal enclave, teaching mathematics to the sons of the Duke of Guise and living on the fee. It is how a younger son with a degree and no living gets across Europe: he sells the arts course back to noblemen, a household at a time. The Guise are the great Catholic house of the French wars, lately at the head of the League, and the young Englishman in their schoolroom is a Protestant subject of Elizabeth. The DNB alone reports it, and reports it without a document.
suggested_refs: The Guise household accounts for the years around 1600, if any survive

stops.name: Marseille: the road along the coast
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; no consulted source dates or documents this leg, and Wikipedia states the itinerary is undocumented in detail
stops.campa: The itinerary through Provence to the sea belongs to the biographers rather than to any register. What he is doing in these years is legible only in what he knows at the end of them: distillation, the sympathies between metals, the doctrine that a man is a small copy of the world he stands in. None of that was on offer at Oxford in 1598. He moves between engagements the way tutors move, a season here, a household there, down to a harbour where ships are loading for Italy and for Spain.
suggested_refs: The Provençal leg of the continental years, undocumented in any consulted source

stops.name: Madrid: through Spain
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the DNB names Spain, later accounts name Madrid, and no document places him in either
stops.campa: Spain is second in the DNB's list of four countries, and nothing else about it survives. An English traveller crossing the Spain of the Inquisition in the last years of a war between the two crowns is either well connected or extremely careful, and the sources say neither. Later accounts fill the blank with Madrid, the court city of Philip III, on the reasoning that a traveller of standing would have gone there. It may be right. It is not evidence.
suggested_refs: The Spanish leg, named as a country and nothing more

stops.name: Rome: the Italian leg
stops.date_confidence: tradition; Wikipedia states the Italian itinerary is undocumented in detail
stops.campa: Italy is the third country on the list. Rome is where later writers place him, among physicians and apothecaries and the alchemical talk of a city that has learned to keep its hermetic reading quiet. Fludd names no Roman teacher anywhere in his works. What he will publish is built out of exactly this material: Hermes Trismegistus, the Cabala turned Christian, the planet that governs each organ of the body, the world as one instrument. Where he first read it, and from whom, nobody set down.
suggested_refs: Roman alchemical and Paracelsian circles at the turn of the seventeenth century

stops.name: Marburg: the German Paracelsians
stops.date_confidence: the German leg is attested only as 'Germany'. Marburg is a modern stand-in for a documented centre of Paracelsian teaching, not a place Fludd is known to have visited, and the date is the year of his return
stops.campa: The last country on the list is Germany, and Germany is where the medicine he wants is taught in daylight. Marburg has a chair for it; its landgrave pays for chemical physic while other faculties still forbid the books. Which German towns Fludd actually saw is nowhere recorded, and Marburg is where the teaching was rather than anywhere he is known to have slept. He has been abroad six years and holds no degree in medicine. He turns for England in 1604.
suggested_refs: The Marburg chair of chymiatria, founded under Landgrave Moritz of Hesse-Kassel

stops.name: Christ Church, Oxford: back for the medical degree
stops.date_confidence: matriculation at Christ Church attested for 1604; the supplication of 14 May 1605 is given by Wikipedia without a document; the degrees of 16 May 1605 are attested
stops.campa: He comes home and does the thing properly. Christ Church admits him in 1604; on the fourteenth of May the next year he supplicates for the medical degree, and on the sixteenth he is bachelor and doctor of medicine in the same week. The Continent gave him Paracelsus and the sympathies. Oxford gives him the licence to charge for them. Two days, two degrees, and the supplication itself survives only as a date in a modern encyclopedia entry, with no document named behind it.
suggested_refs: The Christ Church matriculation register, 1604; the supplication of 14 May 1605

stops.name: Fenchurch Street: the practice
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He takes a house on Fenchurch Street in the eastern City and sets up as a physician. The practice grows, and the prescriptions will pay for the folios. Thomas Fuller, writing afterwards, explains the success by the patients rather than by the pharmacy: they believed in the man, and the belief made the drugs work. In a city whose College still teaches Galen as the floor of the profession, he keeps an amanuensis and his own apothecary, and has his remedies compounded on Paracelsian lines under his own eye.
stops.quote: a 'faith-natural' which aided the well working of his drugs
stops.quote_source: Thomas Fuller, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), 'Fludd, Robert'
suggested_refs: The Fenchurch Street house, base of a thirty-two year London practice

stops.name: The City of London: admitted after six refusals
stops.date_confidence: the DNB gives election as fellow on 20 September 1609; Wikipedia gives only the month. The College then sat in Linacre's house in Knightrider Street and did not move to Amen Corner until 1614, so this pin is a City locator and not the building
stops.campa: The College of Physicians refuses him at least six times before it takes him. He is examined, admonished in March 1608, examined again. Once inside he becomes an officer of the body that had kept him out, and holds the office four times. The objection was never his learning. It was his contempt for the ordinary course of medicine and his open Paracelsian talk, delivered in Latin to men who took Galen for the ground of the art. At last the annals record one word against his name: dignus, worthy.
stops.quote_source: Verdict of the College of Physicians examiners, recorded in the College annals and quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), 'Fludd, Robert'
suggested_refs: The Annals of the College of Physicians, 1605-1609, recording six rejections and two admonishments

stops.name: Amen Corner: the visitation of the apothecaries
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown. The College moves to Amen Corner in this year
stops.campa: The College, newly housed at Amen Corner in the shadow of Paul's, sends its fellows through the shops of the apothecaries to see what is being sold in the city as medicine. Fludd goes with them, opening jars, condemning stock, signing off on other men's compounds. The physician whose own remedies half the faculty finds suspect is now among those judging the trade. Four years later he helps write the Pharmacopoeia Londinensis, which fixes what a London apothecary may compound and how.
suggested_refs: The 1614 visitation of London apothecaries by the College of Physicians

stops.name: Amen Corner: Censor of the College
stops.date_confidence: 1618 attested; he holds the office again in 1627, 1633 and 1634
stops.campa: Censor is the office that examines candidates and prosecutes unlicensed practice, the same power that was turned against him for six years and is now in his hand. Abroad he is by now a scandal and a name in a pamphlet war; at home he dines at the College and signs its certificates. In the same year the Pharmacopoeia Londinensis goes to press with his work in it. He is forty-four years old. He holds the censorship in 1618, and again in 1627, 1633 and 1634.
stops.quote: one of the most Christian philosophers that ever writ
stops.quote_source: John Webster, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), 'Fludd, Robert'
suggested_refs: The Pharmacopoeia Londinensis of 1618
The Censors' book of the College of Physicians

segments.name: The Fraternity of the Rose Cross

stops.name: Kassel: the manifestos come off the press
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Fama Fraternitatis at Kassel in 1614, the Confessio in 1615
stops.campa: A press at Kassel prints an anonymous pamphlet announcing an invisible brotherhood: a founder named Christian Rosenkreuz dead a hundred and twenty years, a vault opened and found entire, a knowledge of medicine and of nature to be shared freely with anyone who asks for it. The Confessio follows the next year. Across Europe men publish open letters to an address that does not exist, and one of them is a London physician who has never met a Rosicrucian in his life. Nobody who answers the summons ever receives a reply.
suggested_refs: Fama Fraternitatis, Kassel 1614
Confessio Fraternitatis, Kassel 1615

stops.name: Coburg: Libavius attacks the brotherhood
stops.date_confidence: year attested; Libavius lived at Coburg from 1607 until his death in 1616, which is why this pin replaces the centroid of Germany carried in the research pool
stops.campa: Andreas Libavius, chemist and rector of the Gymnasium at Coburg, publishes an analysis of the Confessio and takes the fraternity apart clause by clause: poor Latin, worse theology, a promise of universal reformation from men who will not give their names. He is the most respectable chemist in Germany and no friend of the Paracelsians, and his pamphlet is the one that pulls the London physician into print. Libavius holds the rectorship at Coburg from 1607. He dies there in 1616.
suggested_refs: Andreas Libavius, Analysis confessionis Fraternitatis de Rosea Cruce, 1615

stops.name: Leiden: the Apologia Compendiaria
stops.date_confidence: year attested; printed at Leiden, not in England as the tract is often said to have been
stops.campa: The first defence is printed at Leiden, in Latin, by a man with no Rosicrucian correspondent and no proof the fraternity exists: a compendious apology washing away, as the title puts it, the stains of suspicion and infamy cast upon the brotherhood. He does not claim membership. He argues that what the manifestos teach, the reading of the world as a book of correspondences, is true whether or not their authors are, and that to condemn them is to condemn that.
suggested_refs: Apologia Compendiaria, Fraternitatem de Rosea Cruce Suspicionis et Infamiae Maculis Aspersam, Leiden 1616

stops.name: Leiden: the Tractatus Apologeticus
stops.date_confidence: year attested; Leiden imprint, distinct from the Tractatus Theologo-philosophicus printed at Oppenheim in the same year
stops.campa: A longer tract follows from the same press, defending the integrity of the society at book length. In Germany that April a witness named Justus Helt testifies that the brotherhood's theosophy is neither popish nor Lutheran but Calvinist theology, which is one way of admitting that nobody knows what it is. Fludd's own word for the learning he writes against, the Aristotle and the pagan schoolmen, is ethnic philosophy. What he wants is a natural science that begins at the first chapter of Genesis.
stops.quote_source: Justus Helt, testimony of 20 April 1617, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), 'Fludd, Robert'
suggested_refs: Tractatus Apologeticus integritatem Societatis de Rosea Cruce defendens, Leiden 1617

stops.name: Oppenheim: the de Bry press takes him on
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the Tractatus Theologo-philosophicus; month unknown
stops.campa: The third book of 1617 goes to Oppenheim in the Palatinate, to Johann Theodor de Bry, engraver and printer, whose workshop can cut the plates Fludd's arguments require. Matthaeus Merian is working in that shop through these years and marries de Bry's daughter in this one; which hands cut which of Fludd's diagrams is nowhere recorded, and the traditional attribution to Merian rests on the workshop and not on a signature. The partnership formed here will run seven years.
suggested_refs: Tractatus Theologo-philosophicus, Oppenheim 1617
The workshop of Johann Theodor de Bry at Oppenheim, 1616-1620

segments.name: The History of the Two Worlds

stops.name: Oppenheim: Utriusque Cosmi Historia begins
stops.date_confidence: publication begins in 1617 and runs to 1624 by the imprint; one lens of the research pool ends the run at 1621, and that disagreement is left standing. The month is arbitrary, set to place the volume after the Oppenheim tracts
stops.campa: The book he has been building since the Pyrenees begins to come off the press: the metaphysical, physical and technical history of both worlds, the greater and the lesser. It is issued in instalments over the next seven years, volume after volume, and it makes his name across the Empire while London still knows him as a doctor in Fenchurch Street. The engravings set a man's body inside the circles of the heavens, organ answering to planet; on one plate an astrologer bends over a table of houses, casting a horoscope.
stops.quote: O natura naturans, infinita et gloriosa
stops.quote_source: Fludd's dedication to an unnamed work of 1617, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), 'Fludd, Robert', where the words are said to address the deity
suggested_refs: Utriusque Cosmi, Maioris scilicet et Minoris, Metaphysica, Physica atque Technica Historia, Oppenheim and Frankfurt, 1617-1624

stops.name: Oppenheim: De Musica Mundana
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: Within the great history comes the section on the music of the world, where the cosmos is drawn as a single string stretched from the earth to the highest heaven and divided at the intervals of the octave and the fifth. The elements, the planets, the ranks of angels fall at the fret positions. In Linz an imperial mathematician is finishing a book on the same subject. Fludd is not speaking in metaphor. The proportions that make a consonance are the proportions God worked in, and to hear the one is to know the other.
suggested_refs: De Musica Mundana, within the Utriusque Cosmi Historia, Oppenheim 1618
The divine monochord plate

stops.name: London: the water screw that will not stop
stops.date_confidence: 1618 attested for this specific device, which the research pool had misdated to 1630; Wikipedia separately records that in 1630 he proposed many perpetual motion machines
stops.campa: He draws a mill: a wheel turned by falling water, the water caught below and lifted back to the header tank by an Archimedes screw geared to the same wheel, so that the machine feeds itself and turns forever. The drawing survives, and it is the first such device anyone is known to have set down on paper. Nothing built from it ever turned. It cannot work, and the reason it cannot work is the very principle his opponents will spend the next decade insisting on, that the quantities must balance.
suggested_refs: The 1618 water-screw perpetual motion design, the earliest known description of such a machine

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: the fair and the rest of the two worlds
stops.date_confidence: the run continues at Frankfurt to 1624 by the imprint; one lens of the research pool ends it at 1621
stops.campa: Publication shifts to Frankfurt, where the book fair is the clearing house of European printing and a folio can be in Paris, Prague and London within the season. Copies reach exactly the men who are going to write against him. Fludd never crosses the Channel to see a page of it printed. The de Bry press moves to Frankfurt; Caspar Rötel prints the later parts. By 1624 the history of the two worlds fills volume upon volume of text and engraved plate.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt book fair as distribution channel for the Utriusque Cosmi
Caspar Rötel, printer of the later parts

stops.name: Linz: Kepler answers in the Harmonice Mundi
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the DNB locates the attack in an appendix to the Harmonice Mundi
stops.campa: Johannes Kepler, imperial mathematician, publishes at Linz the five books on the harmony of the world and appends to them an attack on the Englishman. The two men want the same thing: proof that the cosmos is built on musical proportion. Each reads the other's method as the ruin of the subject. Kepler takes his from the angular speeds of the planets at aphelion and perihelion, measured, calculated, printed as intervals a choir could sing. Fludd takes his from a drawing of one string with a hand on the peg.
stops.quote_source: Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), 'Fludd, Robert', citing Johannes Kepler
suggested_refs: Johannes Kepler, Harmonice Mundi, Linz 1619, and its appendix against Fludd

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: Veritatis Proscenium
stops.date_confidence: year attested
stops.campa: The reply comes out at Frankfurt in 1621, under the title of the forestage of truth. Fludd's case is that Kepler has measured the outside of things and called it the whole. Mathematics of the vulgar sort, he says, handles the shadow; the chemical and hermetic way goes at the substance, because it works in what the world is made of and not in the quantity of it. Neither man gives an inch. Kepler answers the year after with an apologia for his own book.
suggested_refs: Veritatis Proscenium, Frankfurt 1621

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: Monochordon Mundi Symphoniacum
stops.date_confidence: year attested; Kepler's rejoinder of the same year is the Pro suo opere Harmonices mundi apologia, not a work called Mathematice as some bibliographies imply
stops.campa: The monochord of the world, sounding together: a whole book on the one string. He sets out again the divisions that put earth at the bottom of the scale and the angelic orders at the top, and answers Kepler point by point. Historians will keep returning to the exchange for three hundred years, as the place where the measured and the emblematic readings of nature come apart. Both men hold that the world is made in tune. They disagree about what you measure to prove it.
suggested_refs: Monochordon Mundi Symphoniacum, Frankfurt 1622
Kepler, Pro suo opere Harmonices mundi apologia, 1622

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: Anatomiae Amphitheatrum
stops.date_confidence: year attested
stops.campa: The anatomical amphitheatre appears at Frankfurt with the monochord reprinted inside it: the opened body and the tuned string bound in one volume, because to him they are one subject taken at two scales. He is a fellow of the College of Physicians and has stood at anatomies in London. The book sells, the Frankfurt fair carries it, and in Paris a friar is already reading him with a pen in his hand. What he wants out of a corpse is not the mechanism.
suggested_refs: Anatomiae Amphitheatrum, Frankfurt 1623

stops.name: Paris: Mersenne opens the second war
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the Quaestiones; the text itself was not read for this journey and is carried as a title
stops.campa: Marin Mersenne, Minim friar, publishes his celebrated questions on Genesis and gives a great part of the book to the Englishman: Fludd is a magician, his cosmology is heresy dressed as physics, his God cannot be told apart from the world. Mersenne is answering a panic as much as a book. The city is still uneasy from the placards posted the year before by deputies of the College of the Rose Cross, announcing an invisible fraternity walking the streets of Paris. He will not let the quarrel go for six years.
stops.quote_source: Marin Mersenne (1623), title cited in Wikipedia, 'Robert Fludd'; the polemical text itself was not verified
suggested_refs: Marin Mersenne, Quaestiones Celeberrimae in Genesim, Paris 1623
The Paris Rosicrucian placards of 1622

stops.name: London: the reply to Patrick Scot that stays in manuscript
stops.date_confidence: 1623 is the date of Scot's book; Fludd's answer is undated and was never printed in his lifetime
stops.campa: Patrick Scot's Tillage of Light attacks alchemy in English, for English readers, and Fludd writes an answer. It never goes to a printer. The manuscript, A Philosophicall Key, sits at Trinity College in Cambridge until Allen Debus transcribes and publishes it in 1979, three hundred and fifty-six years later. It is the one place he argues his case in his own language, to his own countrymen. Why he printed everything else and not this is nowhere recorded.
suggested_refs: A Philosophicall Key, manuscript at Trinity College, Cambridge
Allen G. Debus, Robert Fludd and his Philosophicall Key (1979)
sources: OpenLibrary record for Debus, Robert Fludd and his Philosophicall Key

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: Philosophia Sacra, dedicated to a bishop
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the dedicatee is John Williams, in 1626 Bishop of Lincoln and Dean of Westminster, and not Archbishop of York until 1641
stops.campa: A cosmic meteorology, sacred and truly Christian: wind, cloud, thunder and comet explained by the two principles he takes out of Genesis, light and darkness contending in every square foot of the air. It is dedicated to John Williams, bishop of Lincoln, a great man lately out of favour at court and shortly to be worse. Fludd is a physician with patients among the great, and his books travel up the ladder at home as well as across the Channel. He is fifty-two and has been in print abroad for ten years.
suggested_refs: Philosophia Sacra et vere Christiana, seu Meteorologia Cosmica, Frankfurt 1626

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: two answers to Mersenne in one year
stops.date_confidence: year attested for both works; month unknown
stops.campa: Wisdom's contest with folly comes out under his own name, and in the same year from the same city the Summum Bonum appears over the name Joachim Frizius, defending the Rosicrucians once more. The pseudonym is not a hiding place so much as a second voice at the same table: it lets him say about the fraternity what a fellow of the College of Physicians might rather not sign in London. Everyone takes Frizius for Fludd. Mersenne takes him for Fludd in print.
suggested_refs: Sophiae cum Moria Certamen, Frankfurt 1629
Summum Bonum, Frankfurt 1629, under the name Joachim Frizius

stops.name: Paris: Gassendi's examination
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the text was not read for this journey and is carried as a title
stops.campa: Mersenne, wanting a heavier gun, asks Pierre Gassendi to go through the Fluddean philosophy properly. The Examen appears in 1630, careful and unhurried and hard to answer on the point that in Fludd's system God, soul and world run into one another until nothing can be distinguished. Between the friar's charge of magic and the priest's charge of confusion, Fludd is being read out of natural philosophy while still alive to reply. Gassendi meanwhile is rebuilding physics out of atoms and void.
stops.quote_source: Pierre Gassendi (1630), title cited in Wikipedia, 'Robert Fludd'; the argued text itself was not verified
suggested_refs: Pierre Gassendi, Examen Philosophiae Fluddanae, Paris 1630

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: Medicina Catholica
stops.date_confidence: published in five parts at Frankfurt between 1629 and 1631; the stop is dated to the end of the run
stops.campa: The catholic medicine, in five parts: the whole of his practice set out as doctrine. Disease comes from outside the body, carried on winds out of the four quarters, and the physician reads a patient as he reads a sky, by signature and by star. Every one of these volumes is set in a language and a country his patients never see. Underneath the diagrams lies twenty-five years of a working London practice: the fees, the amanuensis, the apothecary, the patients who got better.
suggested_refs: Medicina Catholica, Frankfurt 1629-1631, in five parts

stops.name: London: the perpetual motions of 1630
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the proposals in general; the water-screw design belongs to 1618
stops.campa: In 1630 he proposes machine after machine that will run without being fed: wheels, weights, screws returning water to the height it fell from. They are drawn with the same care as his diagrams of the angelic orders, by the same hand. He is not a crank at the edge of his own system; he is at the centre of it. If the world is a single instrument played by one hand, motion has no reason to stop, and a mill ought to be able to imitate the heavens, which have turned since the first day of creation without a miller.
suggested_refs: Fludd's 1630 perpetual motion proposals

stops.name: London: Doctor Fludds Answer unto M. Foster
stops.date_confidence: year attested
stops.campa: William Foster, a parson, has published a sponge to wipe away the weapon-salve: the Paracelsian ointment smeared not on the wound but on the blade that made it, the patient healing at a distance. Foster calls the cure devilish. Fludd answers in English, in London, over his own name, at fifty-seven. The salve works, he says, by the sympathy running through a created world, and to call sympathy the devil's work is to make the devil the author of nature.
suggested_refs: Doctor Fludds Answer vnto M. Foster, London 1631
William Foster, Hoplocrisma-Spongus, 1631

stops.name: London: death in the City
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies on the eighth of September, 1637, sixty-three years old, in the city he has practised in for thirty-two years. The quarrels outlive him and are already going the other way: Mersenne's circle, Gassendi's atoms, the mathematics he called the shadow of the thing. In the house on Fenchurch Street the instruments are a physician's and the library is a magus's, and both belonged to the same man. He has been a fellow of the College for twenty-eight years.
suggested_refs: Fludd's will and the inventory of the Fenchurch Street house

stops.name: Holy Cross, Bearsted: the chancel and the monument
stops.date_confidence: the burial follows the death of 8 September 1637 and its day is not recorded; the date given here is the DNB's date for the erection of the monument
stops.campa: He is carried back into Kent and laid in the chancel of Holy Cross, on Church Lane south of the green, a few fields from the house where he was born. Some twenty folios of Latin, printed in towns he never visited, and then this wall tablet in the village church his father's household filled every Sunday. The monument goes up the following August: an inscription, and the arms of a family that made its standing keeping accounts for the queen's wars. The date cut on it is the tenth of August, 1638.
suggested_refs: The Fludd monument in the chancel of Holy Cross Church, Bearsted, erected 10 August 1638

segments.name: Gouda, Frankfurt, and the Long Rediscovery

stops.name: Gouda: Philosophia Moysaica
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: The Mosaic philosophy is printed in Holland the year after his death, with the Latin answer to Foster's sponge bound alongside it. The argument is the one he began with: that the true physics is in the first chapter of Genesis, light divided from darkness, and everything since is commentary on those verses. An English Mosaicall Philosophy follows at London in 1659, in a decade when English natural philosophy has moved on to the pump and the balance. He has been dead twenty-two years.
suggested_refs: Philosophia Moysaica, Gouda 1638
Mosaicall Philosophy, London 1659

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: the Opera in six volumes
stops.date_confidence: the six-volume arrangement is dated 1638; the appended Clavis Philosophiae et Alchimiae Fluddanae is a separate Frankfurt publication of 1633, not of 1638. Month arbitrary
stops.campa: The folios are gathered at Frankfurt and arranged into six volumes, with the key to the Fluddean philosophy and alchemy, printed five years earlier in the same city, bound in at the end to help anyone trying to enter the system from outside. The author has been dead a year. Six volumes is what an argument looks like once it has stopped moving. For the next two hundred and fifty years the standard verdict on the man inside them is one word: magician.
suggested_refs: Fludd's Opera in six volumes, Frankfurt 1638
Clavis Philosophiae et Alchimiae Fluddanae, Frankfurt 1633

stops.name: London: the Real History of the Rosicrucians
stops.date_confidence: year of Waite's publication; month unknown
stops.campa: The Victorian occult revival goes back to the seventeenth century looking for ancestors and finds him waiting. The verdict comes two hundred and fifty years after the fact, from a writer with a stake in it, and for another century it will be quoted as though a contemporary had said it. Arthur Edward Waite, writing a history of the Rosicrucians, calls him the great English mystical philosopher of his century, a man of immense erudition and, on the evidence of his writings, of extreme personal sanctity.
stops.quote: the great English mystical philosopher of the seventeenth century, a man of immense erudition, of exalted mind, and, to judge by his writings, of extreme personal sanctity
stops.quote_source: Arthur Edward Waite, The Real History of the Rosicrucians (1887), as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Robert Fludd'
suggested_refs: Arthur Edward Waite, The Real History of the Rosicrucians, London 1887

stops.name: Ascona, Monte Verita: Pauli takes up the quarrel
stops.date_confidence: the essay is published in 1952; the Eranos lecture that preceded it is undated in the sources consulted, and the date here is the publication year
stops.campa: Wolfgang Pauli, who found the exclusion principle and could not stop asking where physical ideas come from, takes the Kepler quarrel as his case. His essay follows the archetypes into Kepler's astronomy: an inherited image of the trinity, held before there was any evidence for it, shaping what the man believed he was reading straight off the sky. On the other side of that essay stands Fludd, insisting three hundred years earlier that the picture comes first. The physicist does not say which of them was right.
suggested_refs: Wolfgang Pauli, 'The Influence of Archetypal Ideas on the Scientific Theories of Kepler' (1952)
The Eranos meetings at Ascona

stops.name: Zurich: Naturerklaerung und Psyche
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month arbitrary, set to follow the Ascona stop
stops.campa: Rascher Verlag publishes the Kepler study in one volume with Jung's essay on synchronicity, so that a seventeenth-century argument about whether the world is measured or mirrored arrives in print inside a twentieth-century argument about meaningful coincidence. The pairing is deliberate. What was heresy in 1623 is here a hypothesis with a physicist's name on it. Fludd is the antagonist of the first half, three centuries dead and still cast as the man who would not count. The book is called Naturerklaerung und Psyche.
suggested_refs: Naturerklaerung und Psyche, Rascher Verlag, Zurich 1952

stops.name: London: Frances Yates and the memory theatre
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month unknown
stops.campa: Frances Yates, working at the Warburg Institute, reads the theatre engraved in Fludd's book on memory as a real building: the stage of the Globe, remembered by a man who had walked into it. Her chapter sends theatre historians to a hermetic folio for evidence about Shakespeare's playhouse. The magician of the standard verdict turns out to have been a philosopher with a system that held together, and was wrong. Godwin's monograph follows in 1979 and Huffman's in 1988, both putting him back among the Renaissance Christian neo-Platonists.
suggested_refs: Frances Yates, The Art of Memory (1966), chapter XVI
William H. Huffman, Robert Fludd and the End of the Renaissance (1988)
Joscelyn Godwin, Robert Fludd: Hermetic Philosopher and Surveyor of Two Worlds (1979)
